questions.question_text:
Select the option that shows the correct relationship between Statements (1) and (2) from Maya Angelou's poem, 'When Great Trees Fall':
Statement 1: When great trees fall, the world is left permanently unstable.
Statement 2: In the poem, the natural world is depicted as reacting with fear and uncertainty when great trees fall.

Which of the given options contains the figure of speech that appears in the following line from the poem, 'The Power of Music'?
And in the sky the feathered fly turn turtle while
They're winging,

Why does he do this?

To mock B/ to undermine B
To manipulate the mob
Uses sarcasm and irony to get his message across/ to prove that B was not actually honourable

questions.subject: english_literature

extract.speaker: Antony
extract.context_before: Brutus has just addressed the citizens justifying Caesar's assassination, and Antony now takes the stage to deliver his funeral oration.

questions.question_text:
Which one argument of Antony's do you think had the greatest impact on his listeners? Give a reason to support your answer.
What were the citizens' feelings towards Antony before he began his speech?
How do their feelings towards him change at the end of his speech?
key_points: Caesar was not ambitious (reason: he wept when the poor cried/ he refused the crown/ he enriched Rome's coffers with ransoms of captives)
Caesar wept when the poor cried/ Caesar refused the crown/ Caesar enriched Rome's coffers with ransoms of captives (reason: Caesar was NOT ambitious)
Caesar's mutilated body (reason: Plebians shocked/ moved by the sight)
Caesar's blood-stained robe (Reason: Caesar was courageous/ great General/ didn't deserve such a death)
Caesar's will that proved his love for the citizens (reason: Caesar was generous/ loved the people of Rome)
At first resentful and suspicious/ angry/ hostile (accept synonyms)
Later loyal and supportive (accept synonyms)

argument_with_reason.instruction: Accept any ONE plausible argument from Antony's speech + a reason that logically aligns with the stated argument.

feelings_before.instruction: Citizens were resentful / suspicious / angry / hostile towards Antony before his speech.

feelings_after.instruction: Citizens became loyal / supportive of Antony after his speech.

questions.scheme_text: Personal Response Q: Plausible responses such as: Caesar was not ambitious (reason: he wept when the poor cried/ he refused the crown/ he enriched Rome's coffers with ransoms of captives) / Caesar's mutilated body (reason: Plebians shocked/ moved by the sight) / Caesar's blood-stained robe (Reason: Caesar was courageous/ great General/ didn't deserve such a death) / Caesar's will that proved his love for the citizens (reason: Caesar was generous/ loved the people of Rome) [Any 1] + At first resentful and suspicious/ angry/ hostile (accept synonyms) + Later loyal and supportive (accept synonyms)
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates could not respond well, as the reasoning given did not align with the stated argument. Some candidates misinterpreted the intent of the question (before and after), leading to vague or incorrect answers such as "The people favoured Brutus" and "The people turned against Brutus at the end." Instead of analysing the plebeians' reactions to Antony, several wrote about the mob or the conspirators, which was not what the question aimed to assess.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Help students develop the ability to construct logical arguments by pausing to understand what each question truly requires before answering.

questions.subject: english_literature

extract.text:
Cassius: Then, if we lose this battle,
You are contented to be led in triumph
Through the streets of Rome?

Brutus: No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman,
That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome;
He bears too great a mind. But this same day
Must end that work the ides of March begun;
And whether we shall meet again I know not.
Therefore our everlasting farewell take:
Forever, and forever, farewell, Cassius.
If we do meet again, why, we shall smile;
If not, why then, this parting was well made.
extract.speaker: Cassius and Brutus
extract.context_before: Before the Battle of Philippi, Cassius and Brutus exchange farewells, uncertain whether they will survive the coming battle against Antony and Octavius.

questions.question_text:
Why does Brutus say, 'No, Cassius, no'?
What conditions may force Brutus to go bound to Rome?
Brutus says, 'And whether we shall meet again I know not.' What do these words imply?
key_points: In response to question posed by Cassius/was not willing to accept the humiliation of defeat/ to be led as captive/ prisoner through Rome
If they lose the battle/ defeated/ taken captive
Implies uncertainty/ unsure/ doubtful of outcome of battle/ one or the other might die in the battle/ resigned to their fate

why_no.instruction: In response to Cassius's question / was not willing to accept the humiliation of defeat / to be led as captive / prisoner through Rome.

conditions.instruction: If they lose the battle / defeated / taken captive.

implication.instruction: Implies uncertainty / unsure / doubtful of outcome of battle / one or the other might die in the battle / resigned to their fate.

questions.scheme_text: In response to question posed by Cassius/was not willing to accept the humiliation of defeat/ to be led as captive/ prisoner through Rome / If they lose the battle/ defeated/ taken captive / Implies uncertainty/ unsure/ doubtful of outcome of battle/ one or the other might die in the battle/ resigned to their fate
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates struggled to provide accurate and precise responses, leading to a significant loss of marks. Several copied details verbatim from the passage instead of demonstrating comprehension and analysis. In particular, many were unable to answer the second part of the question on 'go bound' correctly, which further contributed to mark deductions.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Incorporate questions that promote higher-order thinking (HOTS) to regular classroom teaching and learning. Train students to read questions carefully, paying attention to specific clue words that indicate what is expected.

questions.teacher_suggestion: Encourage students to highlight or mark important lines in their textbooks for better recall and understanding. Enable students to analyse, evaluate, compare and contrast characters and thematic inter-textuality for more thorough reading of literary texts.

questions.examiner_comment: (a) Many candidates merely rephrased the lines without analysing their deeper meaning. They struggled to explain the ideas in their own words and were unable to express their thoughts clearly. (b) Many candidates restated the lines in different words but did not explore their deeper meaning. The word 'divine' was often misunderstood, leading to incorrect interpretations. (c) Some candidates failed to clearly explain why the King felt they were safer 'here' (seated in the gallery, away from the lions in the pit) than 'there' (in the arena among the fighting lions).
questions.teacher_suggestion: Emphasise word meanings in context, not in isolation, and encourage inference and interpretation while teaching the text. Guide students to read and understand every line of a poem rather than relying on summaries. Reinforce careful reading and clear understanding of each question before answering.
